PD psychology program 
Introduction
This psychological program is designed as an integrated component of a broader digital therapeutic experience for people with Parkinson’s disease (PwP). Its purpose is not only to address psychological symptoms, but also to support the day-to-day behaviors that make multidisciplinary treatment effective over time. The psychological program is intended to help users 1) cope more effectively with the emotional and psychological burden of PD, through a supportive framework and a toolkit of relevant practices that users can learn practice and integrate into daily life; 2) engage with movement, physical therapy, speech therapy, occupational therapy, cognitive training, and medication-management; and 3) build a sustainable daily routine that can continue after the initial structured 12-week phase. Notably, the app is not trying to deliver a traditional therapist-led CBT or mindfulness course. It is trying to support daily participation in a complex rehabilitation environment, with no live therapist and minimal writing or conversational interaction.
Clinical rationale
Parkinson's affects a wide range of emotional, cognitive, and behavioral processes. People living with Parkinson’s often face challenges such as anxiety, depression, emotional dysregulation, attention difficulties, apathy, reduced motivation, identity shifts, and adjustment difficulties related to the disease’s progression and its impact on daily life. In more advanced stages, there can also be psychosis (as an undesired result of the dopaminergic treatment), impulse control issues, and cognitive decline. 
These "non-motor symptoms" are in part shaped by the experience of living with PD, but many of them are direct symptoms of the condition itself – often appearing before the motor symptoms. They can significantly affect quality of life, independence, daily functioning, relationships, and adherence to the therapeutic program. They can even amplify motor symptoms (for example - anxiety or sleep difficulties may exacerbate tremors and freezing), creating a reinforcing cycle of distress and functional decline.
A psychological component is especially important in PD because emotional and motivational difficulties are not peripheral to the condition. Anxiety, low mood, stress, apathy, shame, guilt reduced confidence, and social withdrawal can all interfere with rehabilitation and daily functioning. The program acknowledges and validates these challenges, bringing them into awareness while offering practical ways to respond, alongside a sense of support and encouragement. The central challenge this psychological program is designed to address is not just “mental health symptoms,” but the moment-to-moment gap between intention and action. A user may value movement, believe it is important, and still fail to begin. They may want to use the speech program but avoid it because of embarrassment or low confidence. They may know that sleep affects tomorrow’s functioning but fail to implement a settling routine because the day already feels like a loss. The program is designed around these gaps.
The program combines several therapeutic traditions in a practical way:
CBT-informed elements are used for unhelpful thoughts, worry, self-criticism, sleep, and practical coping. 
Behavioral activation is used to address apathy, reduced activity, low momentum, and the tendency to wait for motivation before acting. 
Mindfulness and physiological regulation are used to help users settle stress and re-engage attention. 
ACT (acceptance and commitment therapy)-informed elements are introduced in simplified form to support purpose, willingness, values-based action, and psychological flexibility. 
Self-compassion and pacing are used to reduce boom-bust cycles, shame, and dropout after difficult days. 
Graded confidence-building is used to support participation in movement, speech, cognition, and social action. 
This combination is especially appropriate in PD because the app needs to support both emotional wellbeing and adherence behavior. In addition, to some extent, there is an aspect of a journey to the psychological content, with later content building upon earlier concepts, allowing users to gradually expand their skills, understanding, and application over time.
In addition, the program incorporates two supporting approaches that are useful in a non-conversational, therapist-free digital environment.
The first is an MI-informed motivational layer. The app does not attempt to replicate formal motivational interviewing, since it cannot provide live reflective listening or responsive dialogue. Instead, it uses structured MI-consistent elements: eliciting personally meaningful reasons, acknowledging ambivalence without confrontation, supporting autonomy, strengthening confidence, and helping users choose the next step rather than merely deciding whether or not to act. This is designed to increase adherence and persistence, which are shaped by self-efficacy, confidence, meaning, fatigue, and support as much as by knowledge of what is “good to do.”
The second is the careful use of therapeutic suggestion. This is not formal hypnosis, and the program should not be framed that way. Rather, it uses brief supportive suggestions that shape attention, bodily settling, expectancy, and readiness for action. In practice, this means language that helps users orient to the present moment, soften bodily tension, anticipate manageable success, and enter tasks with less friction. Suggestive wording is particularly well suited to audio-guided practices, calming sequences, and confidence-building prompts. In a condition where initiation, bodily tension, uncertainty, and symptom-related apprehension can all interfere with action, such phrasing can make the psychological layer feel more immediate and embodied. Suggestive language should be used to support attention, calm, confidence, and readiness, not to make unrealistic promises or imply magical control over symptoms. Suitable uses include:
settling the body before tasks 
post-practice prompts 
increasing expectancy of manageable success 
focusing attention on one step at a time 
softening self-critical interpretations 
reinforcing bodily cues of readiness 
pleasant familiarity over different practices (voice, movement, etc.) starting with a pleasant welcome, taking a calming breath, ending with a thank you, an encouragement, or a "for the rest of the day…".
Importantly, the program also aims to strengthen users' perception that every interaction with the app is itself a meaningful act of managing their Parkinson's. The messaging and overall tone should help users recognize that every practice they complete, every activity they engage in, and every time they return to the app is already an active step toward better self-management, healthier habits, and improved daily functioning. Over time, the app should reinforce the feeling that "I am someone who is actively doing something for my health," helping users see themselves as more active, engaged, and capable.
Because Parkinson’s disease is highly variable, the psychological program is intentionally broad. It is designed to address a wide range of emotional, cognitive, and functional challenges that people with Parkinson’s may face in daily life. The program aims to better equip users with knowledge, tools, habits, and practical strategies to manage difficulties (unhelpful emotional and cognitive patterns, harmful habits or self-talk and more) or positively put- living healthier life with PD and improving quality of life.
While some patients may also develop deeper insight as a result of the psychology program, in essence it is mainly trying to produce:
lower self-blame 
higher self-efficacy
higher willingness to start 
better emotional regulation before tasks 
more flexible persistence on bad days 
stronger identity and meaning around continued practice 
long-term habit formation with a low burden interface
Increased involvement with life
Note that the same principles and language can and should be consistently applied not only within the psychological program but also within all the other programs in the app (physical therapy, occupational therapy, dance therapy, speech therapy, cognitive training, etc.). 

Design Principles
The psychological program has a “standalone” component to it, but it is also an adherence engine - The psychology layer should support use of the rest of the app. It should not feel like “extra homework” competing with the rehabilitation content.
Daily interaction should be low-burden and mostly non-writing based - The program is designed for video, audio, games, and tap-based input. Free-text writing is minimized. This is especially appropriate for PD because handwriting, typing, fatigue, and cognitive load can all make long journaling tasks impractical, especially in a self-guided format. 
In line with the approach taken across the entire therapeutic program, the psychological program emphasizes learning with application. Ideally, each concept, technique, or therapeutic principle introduced is accompanied by opportunities for practice and integration. This may take the form of interactive exercises, structured reflections, or real-life tasks that are brought back into the app through self-reporting and feedback. The goal (and challenge) is to make therapeutic content not only informative, but usable, engaging, and relevant to users’ daily experiences. 
Safety and escalation need to be built in - Because the app is self-guided, it should include basic information on when to seek additional support, including in mental health aspects (severe anxiety, depression, hallucinations, etc.,). This can also be referred throughout the program in places where it makes sense to (e.g., in the unit talking about anxiety).  
Theme (within the first 12 weeks) - Each unit focuses on one main psychological or behavioral skill, taught through one anchor “lesson” and repeated daily micro-practices.
Logic for missed days – the anchor should be prioritized and not to be missed. 
Program High-Level Structure
The psychological program is organized into units, each addressing specific themes, topics, or therapeutic targets relevant to individuals living with Parkinson’s. Notably, the psychological program follows a more linear and progressive structure compared to other domains, at least in the initial 12 weeks, which are more structured. As we move to the maintenance phase, users can continue to practice the psychological tools and routines they most connected with. 
In the first 12 weeks, each unit has one main theme, but the theme is taught through repetition and practical use. The unit rhythm is:
one “anchor lesson” at the start of the unit- ± 3 minutes long
one related short daily interaction 
Some of these will be additional “learning” to reinforce the message and place it in additional contexts
Some of these will be practices that can be used repeatedly over time - also beyond the unit in which they were introduced --> note that some of the practices are longer (up to 7 minutes), will be marked below as longer
optional additional content patients can access if interested 
In addition, the themes can be used within other modules in the app (e.g., the physiotherapist can speak about action before motivation, the occupational therapist can refer to pacing, etc.) + they can inform reusable boosters linked to that unit’s theme – see above the note about creating visuals that can be repeated throughout the app.
The intention is that users meet the same ideas in slightly different forms: watch it once, practice it repeatedly, use it while doing other therapy, and then eventually internalize it as part of their routine. While it is expected that the “learning” sections will not necessarily be something the patients go back to, the practices should be designed to be used repeatedly. 
Types of activities
The psychology program includes the following types of assets:
Educational – these are designed to provide information. They may be delivered in various formats, such as video, animated video, slides, articles, etc. They are passive in nature and are not designed to be used many times. 
Practices – these are designed as tools that the patients that they learn and repeat over time, as self-care tools. These can be, for example, breathing exercises, relaxation/mindfulness audios, collecting a positive moment, etc.  
Interactive- these are designed to help patients internalize the education they have been exposed to. The goal is to turn them from passive viewers to more active “learners”. These may include, for example – asking a question and letting the patient choose from a list of answers, adopting certain ideas/thoughts and rejecting others, marking a key idea to “keep” etc. These mechanisms may be shared across modules. They are not designed as self-help tools or activities that the patient is likely to go back to and can follow the educational or the practice content. 
Visual anchors – this is a part of the educational content, however it is spelled out separately because of its importance and applicability beyond the piece of educational content it appears in originally. The idea is to create several key visual anchors. For example, show a visual of a bull’s eye to signify how close an action is to core values, and then use the visual later when asking about value-guided actions in the daily protocol. Or use a visual of an imbalance between perceived effort and perceived reward when explaining apathy, and then repeat this visual when the physical therapist talks about the daily physio practice. 
A focus on practices  
The psychological content is structured into modules (weeks), each covering themes that support the patient journey. Alongside the modules, users are introduced to practices that they learn and repeat over time, either in their original form or with variations adapted to each module’s theme. These practices also function as standalone self-care tools.
Conceptual note: The practices are connected and support each other. Each emphasizes a different aspect of mind–body regulation while supporting the others.
Relaxation practices emphasize ease and physical comfort, which supports breathing and mindfulness. 
Breathing practices are embedded within both relaxation and mindfulness that often call for intentional breathing. 
Mindfulness introduces acceptance and non-judgmental awareness, which enhances the effectiveness of both relaxation and breathing practices.
Core/optional practices
Core practices are integrated into daily activities and repeated throughout the program, sometimes with variations aligned to module themes. 
Additional practices are offered for users who want to deepen their engagement, understanding, and practice.(e.g., after practicing two short breathing exercises, the user can access two additional optional breathing techniques; or after practicing guided imagery for relaxation, the user can try guided imagery for a safe place or a longer version for sleep).
Structure of practices
Practices include the following components:
Intro
core things to remember
Practice
The first time the practice is introduced, it will be introduced with all parts.  
In the library (or wherever else the user will be able to go back to the practice) the user should be able to skip the intro. 
Practice overview (high-level)

Note - For breathing exercises – there are additional requirements related to including audio and allowing change of pace. See document  Breathing Exercises- design and implementation input.docx
Note – for exploring a pleasant experience, self- compassion moment, gratitude moment - See document Reflective and emotional practices for App C and PD App.docx
Note – the connection card game required further specification. Two ideas Renan suggested (in addition to suggesting the concept in the first place) were rolling dice to choose (maybe choose a themed pile?) and displaying a “card” with prompts on both sides so that if someone sits across someone else they can see it at the same time.  
Practice frequency
Three practices per week are ideal to ensure meaningful exposure and engagement. There is no need for users to practice all types or specific categories; after initial exposure, it may be more beneficial for them to practice regularly what feels most suitable and relevant to them (choice).
Practice timing – open question
Ideally, some practices would be timed to be practiced at the end of the day. Open question – can that be done
Personalization – to be specified
Over time, the app could personalize practice recommendations based on user preferences (e.g., breathing, relaxation, mindfulness, cognitive practices). For this purpose, the app would need to collect the user’s rating of each practice. Details are TBD. 
Continuing with practices after the 12 weeks – open question
Ideally, users will be able to continue using the practices after the 12 weeks protocol. This is outside the scope of this document, however if a general plan is put in place to address longer-term use, the psychological practices should be part of it, based on the table of practices. 
Thoughts for after the 12 weeks (new section) 
Current assumption is that after the 12 weeks the program will simply continue. This means that
week 12 does not have to be a “let’s collect our thoughts and summarize” week. 
We should have a repetitive structure that can be used over time after week 12 too
Suggestion – a 7 day structure, in which there is:
Day 1 – choice between relaxation exercises: PMR, guided imagery relaxation, guided imagery safe place, grounding
Day 2 – choice between breathing exercises: belly, square, coherent, sigh
Day 3 – choice between “self-care” reflections – gratitude, self-compassion, pleasant moment, I am enough audio
Day 4 – choice between mindfulness exercises – awareness of breath, body scan, observing thoughts, mindful eating, mindful walking, attention to hands and feet  
Day 5 – Card game (can be self reflection or with someone)
Day 6 – combined inner voice workout 
Day 7 – choice between in-the-moment tools to practice – one breath reset, soften one place, three anchors 
Thought – if this is the “end game”, we should strive to make the program gradually shift to this structure, and have less education pieces unless they are crucial for the motivation/good practice, moving the rest to the library

A focus on non-practice interactions
(note – practices are in the previous section, some of them are interactive)
Cognitive Training Interaction: Working with Thoughts (thoughts game)
Several units in the psychological program involve identifying and working with thoughts/self talk- whether biased, unhelpful, validating, or self-compassionate. While users receive psychoeducation and reflection, a gamified component can deepen this work by providing repetitive, engaging training that supports cognitive flexibility, emotional distancing (defusion), and internalization of more adaptive inner voice. Importantly, there is an evidence base for the efficacy of this sort of game suggested here (see the work of Guy Doron). 
The core concept is:
we present the user with a “sorting task” of thoughts. Each time the task is different, based on the specific unit we are in. For example, in the “thoughts are not commands” unit, the user will need to identify biased thoughts versus non-biased thoughts. In the “self care” unit, the user will need to identify thoughts that promote self compassion  versus thoughts that do not promote it. 
We can also mix a few tasks together from several units.  
the user should get feedback if they identified correctly or not. 
Core therapeutic principles supported:
Repeated exposure to maladaptive vs. adaptive statements
Reinforcement of adaptive thinking and self-talk
Defusion through repetition, labeling, and interaction
Non-declarative learning that supports cognitive flexibility
Key aspects to consider:
This is not a full-blown game with progression/regression, but it can be a powerful way to practice the learned content in a fun and effective manner. 
The most important thing is making it fun and rewarding: Guy Doron's app can be an example for a dull and flat implementation. This deepends on availability of design and creative resources, but in theory there is an opportunity to integrate gamification elements like playful reinforcements, and humor. For example, biased thoughts could appear with exaggerated or caricatured visuals (e.g., the phrase “You’re not good enough” might be spoken by a cartoonish “inner critic” character like an old disapproving aunt). Having a golden statement (like "I'm good enough") that when the user correctly swipe, fills the screen, etc. Using positive imagery and positive reinforcement: positive imagery like brain, trees or clouds in the mechanic. In addition, "correct" responses trigger visual/audio feedback (growth, clarity, affirming messages), but avoid punitive framing for biased thoughts (not to create negative associations). These touches might be the way to make it enjoyable and more memorable.
Swipe mechanic: e.g., accept/reject - was used effectively in research, can be replaced with a different mechanic of course.
Speech integration: Optional - hear thoughts read aloud and/or speak them to deepen processing and externalization.
Progress encouragement: Periodic feedback to reinforce positive change (e.g., “You’re training you inner voice to be more balanced”)
Short, flexible play format: 2–3 minute sessions.
Repeated explanations of the game's rational and desired outcome: direct or via embedded rationale cues like “When you practice this skill, you’re strengthening your resilience.”
Note: In PD this game also engages cognitive aspects like proceeding speed, fine movement and visuospatial abilities, that might need special consideration. 
Personal note from Ariel: I genuinely believe this format holds potential as subtle yet meaningful therapeutic support tool. If designed thoughtfully, it can help bridge the gap between theory and practice, making cognitive work more accessible, engaging, and emotionally resonant for users.
Pre or post-activity reflection
Before or after activities (also outside the psychological program) we may define a reflection. This will be in the form of one of the following:
Showing just text (and the user is invited to think about it)
Note that ideally there would be some mechanism to make sure the user indeed takes a few seconds to think instead of just clicking next
asking a question and letting the patient choose from a list of answers
Note that there can be 1-3 questions per activity
Note that the app should present a feedback based on the answer selected for each question (ideally, we can define a few response options and randomly show one so that the user is not always presented with the same feedback)
Examples – after a mindfulness practice, ask if they feel more relaxed; after the anchor lesson ask a few questions such as “do you ever feel more anxious when your medication starts to wear off? (reply) “do you ever feel that stress makes symptoms more prominent?” (reply) “do you sometimes feel that it is hard to relax? (reply)” and then based on the answers, show a connecting sentence “in the following days we will share some practical tools you can use when …”.  
Logic – the app should allow to define if the post-activity reflection is shown:
Always
Only the first X times this activity is done
Skip option – the app should allow users to skip the reflection and continue to the next activity 
Note that a similar structure can also be used for activities without prior educational content displayed (e.g. - in the first unit, one activity is that the user is reminded of the motivation they chose on day 1 and is invited to reflect how today’s daily activity can be relevant to achieve this motivation)
Note that it makes sense for the app to remember the replies and use this information in the care coordinator. 
Keep
To help facilitate knowledge assimilation, we will offer user the ability to “keep” 1-3 key points from education pieces they view or practices they perform. These will be pre-defined and the user will just be able to select them. 
the user will be able to access these “keeps” in the library, and each “keep” will link to the original education or practice it was taken from. 
Select Motivation
In the first unit, the user will be asked to select a main motivation for using the app (out of a predetermined list)
Consider option to let the user choose up to 3 main motivations 
This app needs to “remember” this selection so that future messaging to the user can relate back to this motivation selection (for example – write a message after completing a physical therapy sequence connecting it with the selected motivation). 
The motivation(s) selected do not need to appear consistently anywhere after the selection (meaning there is no need to display it somewhere or let the user edit it, etc.) 
A note on the care coordinator
The care coordinator should collect the patients’ choices throughout the use of the app and use that to provide patient-specific framing of the activities (both within the psych program and outside of it). For example, if a patient indicates that spending time with family is a strong value/motivation, the care coordinator will use that to create motivational and suggestive introductions to activities within the app (example – working on your strength may feel like a lot sometimes, but remember this is not just a movement goal, you are doing it so that you can have more quality time with your family). 
Out of scopes/open questions 
Out of scope – biofeedback 
We are not integrating any form of biofeedback (e.g., - heart rate, breathing sound via microphone) . It could be powerful but requires significant effort. 
Open question - Mood tracking and integration of the psych program with it: at the moment, we have not determined if there is mood tracking, and at the moment any mood tracking is not directly linked to the psychological program.
Key units in the psychological program:
Program Detailed Structure
Throughout the program, some elements are considered core, while others are optional for those interested in exploring more. 

Unit 1: Welcome
Anchor
a brief explanation that PD affects not only movement (its not all physical symptoms), but also mood, attention, stress, confidence, motivation, energy fluctuation, frustration tolerance, and social comfort and that these are common and understandable consequences of the condition.
These difficulties are not always in the foreground when people think about Parkinson’s or even in medical appointments (people tend to think mainly on the physical symptoms), yet living with them can be complex and burdensome. Addressing them and learning how to respond to them a little more effectively (a little bit every day… small steps make a big difference…) can make a meaningful difference in daily life.
a normalization of common reactions: frustration, grief, worry, slower initiation, embarrassment, reduced spontaneity, self-blame 
The psychological program is designed to help you build practical skills for these different challenges.
Sometimes this means learning how to respond differently to difficult thoughts or worries. 
Sometimes it means learning ways to calm the body or regulate stress. 
Sometimes it means training attention and mindfulness. 
Sometimes it means strengthening self-compassion, confidence, or social participation. 
And sometimes it means finding ways to stay engaged with the people, activities, and values that matter to you. 
Throughout the program, you will learn simple tools, practice them, and might gradually discover which ones work best for you.
Emphasize that the app is built around repetition, flexibility, experimentation, and small steps rather than perfection.
The overall message is that even a few minutes of practice can be a meaningful investment in yourself and your daily life.
***Perhaps we could also note that this is a gradual learning process (a few minutes a day). Each week adds another small piece to the puzzle. On its own, each step may seem simple, but over time these small pieces can add up to something meaningful.
a simple explanation that the app is built around repetition, flexibility, and small steps. The tone should be: there is a target, but we protect continuity. The framing is positive and encouraging: even a few minutes in the app is already a meaningful step, a few minutes invested in self-care.
Reinforce that every interaction with the app is already a meaningful act of managing Parkinson's. we want to frame each completed activity as active participation in one's health, helping users begin to see themselves as people who are actively taking care of themselves. 
Content can and should use stories/examples (e.g., someone who wants to walk more safely, someone who wants to feel more confident speaking, someone who wants to stay connected and independent). 
Daily activities (to be finalized with the prontent team)

Unit 2: Action before motivation 
Anchor: 
Meaningful action often needs to come before motivation feels strong enough. This is especially important in PD, where low momentum, apathy, discouragement, and reduced spontaneity can contribute to a passive loop. 
It's really hard to increase motivation. Waiting for motivation to come is unhelpful and impractical – the common confusion is we often treat motivation as if it’s the fuel we need before we begin. But in many cases, action is what generates motivation, not the other way around. You might start feeling more motivated once you are already engaged in activities.  However, it is possible to get help to get started.
difficulty initiating does not mean laziness or lack of character. The first step is often harder than the second and third (like a train, it is hardest to get moving at the beginning, but once it starts, it carries itself more easily).
explain the cycle in which low action leads to lower confidence and lower mood, which then makes future action less likely. Explain why often the thing that is most within the patient’s control is the action. It should clarify that the app’s own content can count as meaningful action: movement can count as health and accomplishment, speech work can count as connection, cognitive work can count as engagement and competence, and occupational strategies can count as independence. 
Waiting for motivation or the “right” feeling before acting can become a trap. This can happen to anyone, but it is especially relevant in Parkinson’s, where motivation, energy, and mood can fluctuate due to the condition itself. A person may think, “I’ll start when I feel more ready, less tired, or more motivated,” but these internal states are not fully under voluntary control. As a result, action gets delayed. Over time, this leads to less activity, less sense of reward, and less momentum, which can lower mood and confidence and make starting feel even harder.
Note – this is a topic which really would resonate well if presented by the other therapists in the app
Daily activities (to be finalized with the prontent team)

Unit 3+4 (longer unit) Stress, anxiety, and calming the body
Anchor: 
Normalize that stress and anxiety are very common human experiences and part of everyday life. At the same time, when living with ongoing physical challenges, they can become more frequent or more intense. Learning effective ways to regulate stress can therefore become a valuable resource. 
Explain that stress and anxiety can also amplify physical symptoms and increase perceived effort, so being able to calm the body and mind, even a little, can make daily activities feel more manageable. For example, these skills can help get some ease in moments of tension, help you get more out of moments of rest, improve sleep, and make it easier to focus or reconnect with yourself before activity.
Many people do not engage with these tools because they feel inaccessible, unclear, or not suitable for them. This is a chance to explore these skills in a simple and practical way, to try them out, and to find what works for you through direct experience.
Explain that anxiety may appear as the medication wears off for some people. Explain the anxiety wave and how it will naturally come down unless it is ‘fed”. 
Include a brief introduction to mind–body practices as part of the anchor, covering the basic ideas of what these practices are, how they can help, and how they are typically practiced. (More specific guidance and explanations will be provided within the daily activities for each practice, e.g. breathing, relaxation, mindfulness, etc,). Perhaps touching on specific applications and special consideration for PD.
Note - Users will be invited to rate the different practices after completing them. This serves as a brief reflection that helps them notice what felt helpful, relevant, calming, or enjoyable. 
Note – this could also be a way for the app to learn what works best for users and suggest higher rated practices, however if user choice is available this is optional. 
Consistently reinforce that completing a practice is itself meaningful progress. Feedback throughout the app should strengthen the association between using the app and being an active, engaged participant in one's own health and rehabilitation.
Note that this unit has some longer practices
Two brief and engaging introductory explanations will be developed: one for all breathing practices and one for all relaxation practices. These introductions will focus on the rationale, purpose, and general approach to each type of practice. They will be presented only the first time users encounter a breathing or relaxation exercise and will remain accessible for later with practices of that kind.
Individual practices will have only on the instructions, key points, and practical guidance needed for that specific exercise. These will be delivered through brief pre-practice screens and/or audio guidance.
Daily activities (to be finalized with the prontent team)
Unit 5: Thoughts are not commands
Anchor: 
 Provide a brief explanation of common thinking patterns and biases, and how thoughts influence emotions, physical sensations, and ultimately behavior. Emphasize that the mind is constantly generating thoughts, and that learning how to soften the impact of these thoughts and respond to them more flexibly can be very useful in daily life.
Introduces simple cognitive flexibility and defusion.  
The goal is to reduce the power of common unhelpful thoughts enough that the user can proceed with the next step. Loosen the grip of unhelpful thoughts enough to keep moving and understand the role of interpretation
Present a small set of common thoughts in PD: “this won’t help,”  “I’m failing,”, “if  I can’t do it the proper way it's not worth it”, “doing only a few minutes does not count”
a thought can be understandable without being useful, and that the next helpful action does not depend on first eliminating every discouraging thought. 
Introduce the idea of noticing a thought rather than being caught in it (e.g., shifting from “I’m failing” to “I notice I’m having the thought that I’m failing”)
Daily activities (to be finalized with the prontent team)
Unit 6: Mindfulness and present-moment awareness
Anchor 
The anchor lesson should provide a clear and practical foundation for mindfulness, keeping the explanation relevant and grounded without becoming overly theoretical. It may include brief scientific context (including in PD) and simple everyday examples to support understanding and application.
It should explain that the mind often moves into prediction, self-evaluation, discouragement, worries about the future, or regrets about the past. Returning attention to the present moment can help reduce distress and allow for fuller engagement with daily life.
Introduce mindfulness in daily life and its relevance in PD. Practices such as awareness of breath, body scan, mindful walking, and mindful eating can help users respond with awareness rather than react automatically to internal or external stressors. Emphasize that mindfulness is not only a formal practice, but an ongoing way of relating to experience – gently, kindly, and repeatedly bringing attention back to the present moment.
Link this to the broader role of attention in PD. Many actions that were once automatic may require more conscious attention, and learning to direct attention intentionally can support functioning in daily activities, such as walking through narrow spaces or speaking more clearly. In this sense, training attention becomes a meaningful and practical skill.
Throughout the week, highlight that the emphasis is not on doing long or perfect practices, but on cultivating an attitude of patiently returning attention and finding a sustainable rhythm. Mindfulness can be applied directly within everyday activities, and brief practices before tasks (e.g., before walking or eating) may help make these actions feel more manageable and steadier.
Users will be invited to rate the different practices after completing them. This serves both as a brief reflection that helps them notice what felt helpful, relevant, calming, or enjoyable and as a way for the app to learn what works best for them. This allows the app to suggest practices that feel more personally supportive and increases the likelihood of continued use and integration.
Daily activities (to be finalized with the prontent team)
Note – it would be helpful to incorporate the concept also into educational pieces or as part of the practices in physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, dance. Topics like: eating, talking, breathing, walking with big steps, dealing with freezing, daily activity etc. all involve this ability to direct attention and these therapists can mention mindfulness as one way to “train” this attention muscle. 
Unit 7: Self-care: Self-compassion, self-validation, gratitude and exploring pleasant moments 
Anchor
Present the principles of self-compassion, self-validation, gratitude and exploring pleasant moments. Differentiate this from positivity at all costs. 
Explain the importance of self-validation and self-compassion, and how they can support emotional resilience, reduce self-criticism, and make it easier to continue engaging with daily activities. While the concepts can be introduced clearly and directly, the emphasis should remain practical and relatable.
Highlight the benefits from gratitude practice and from exploring pleasant moments, emphasizing that the idea is to focus on normal daily experiences, and not anything “huge”. 
Include a cognitive component that addresses common misconceptions and biases (e.g., “I should be handling this better,” “I don’t deserve rest”) and introduces more supportive and realistic self-talk that can be used in day-to-day situations.

Highlight that self-care is not only about how we think or feel, but also about what we do. This includes intentionally making space in daily life for activities that are meaningful, enjoyable, or nourishing, even in small ways.

Appendix 3 – Apathy resources 
Apathy in PD is increasingly understood not as a mood problem like depression, but as a disorder of motivation and effort-based decision-making. While depression affects how someone feels (sadness, hopelessness), apathy reflects a disruption in the brain’s “cost-benefit calculator". The brain tends to overestimate how much effort a task will require and underestimate how rewarding it will feel. This bias fuels an “Underdo-It” cycle: a person decides it’s too much work to attend a coffee meetup, stays home, receives no rewarding dopamine boost from social interaction, and as a result finds the next activity even harder to initiate. 
Modern cognitive-behavioral approaches for apathy (CBT-A) aim to recalibrate this system by reducing perceived effort (e.g., focusing first on putting on walking shoes rather than completing a full walk), increasing reward saliency significance, and using structured “if-then” plans to bypass impaired initiation. By creating small, achievable “micro-wins” such as committing to just five minutes of activity patients can trigger modest dopamine releases that help gradually restore motivation. 
See paper and video for more details:

The shift toward effort-based decision-making represents a major evolution in how we treat apathy. Historically, doctors treated apathy like depression, but we now know they are neurologically different: depression is a "feeling" problem (sadness), while apathy is a "valuation" problem (the brain decides the reward isn't worth the effort).
In Parkinson's, the brain’s "cost-benefit calculator" becomes biased. Because dopamine levels are low, the brain overestimates how much physical or mental effort a task will take and underestimates how good the reward will feel.
This creates a self-reinforcing loop:
The Trap: "It’s too much work to go to that coffee meetup. I’ll just stay here."
The Result: Because you don't go, you get zero dopamine "spikes" from social interaction.
The Consequence: Your brain's "reward system" remains dormant, making the next task feel even harder. This is the "Underdo-It" Cycle—a downward spiral of inactivity that actually makes the biological apathy worse.
Modern CBT (sometimes called CBT-A for Apathy) focuses on recalibrating this internal calculator. Therapists work on three specific areas:
Cost-Reduction Strategies: If a task feels like it costs 10 units of energy, how can we lower it to 2? 
Example: Instead of "going for a 30-minute walk," the goal is "putting on walking shoes." Once the shoes are on, the "activation energy" required for the walk is significantly lower.
Reward Saliency: Apathetic brains "miss" rewards. Therapists use Savoring Techniques—asking patients to focus intensely on a specific positive detail (the smell of the coffee, the sun on their face) to "force" the brain to acknowledge the reward.
External Scaffolding: Since the brain struggles with internal initiation, CBT-A uses "If-Then" planning (Implementation Intentions). 
Script: "If the clock strikes 10:00 AM, then I will stand up and walk to the kitchen." This moves the decision from the struggling frontal lobe to a more automatic response.
The goal is to create "micro-wins" that provide just enough dopamine to fuel the next small action.
The 5-Minute Rule: Patients are told to commit to an activity for just 5 minutes. Often, the act of starting provides the neurochemical "kick" needed to continue.
Low-Reward Sensitivity Training: Research shows apathetic patients ignore low rewards. CBT-A teaches patients to "stack" rewards. 
Example: Don't just do physical therapy; do physical therapy while listening to a favorite podcast. The podcast provides an immediate, high-probability reward that "subsidizes" the effort of the exercise.

The choice point 
Life is full of challenging situations, thoughts, and feelings (the "storm"). In PD they are also full with motor symptoms, apathy, and more. When these arise, you reach a "fork in the road" (or Choice Point), where you decide whether to take a path that moves you away from your values or towards a rich and meaningful life. Away Moves: Behaving in ways that temporarily avoid or suppress uncomfortable thoughts/feelings but ultimately increase distress and pull you away from your values. Example – social withdrawal.  Towards Moves: Behaving in ways that are consistent with your deepest values, even while experiencing pain. The Goal: The goal is not to eliminate "bad" feelings, but to recognize the choice point and, through mindfulness and "unhooking" techniques, make choices that align with your values.

1,Take a breather,Info-brt-grp-01,"Breathing practices can support regulation while also serving as an anchor for mindful awareness. As you practice, gently notice where and how you feel the breath in the body. "
2,Take a breather,Info-brt-grp-02,"A breathing practice may offer something different each day: focus, relaxation, comfort, or simply a moment to pause. Choose a practice with curiosity and notice what it offers today. "
3,Take a breather,Info-brt-grp-03,"Building a personal toolkit means discovering what fits different moments. Feel free to adjust the breathing pattern, pace, or length to suit your needs today. "
4,Relaxation,Info-rlx-grp-01,"Discomfort can leave the body holding unnecessary tension. As you choose a relaxation practice, notice whether pausing helps you release some effort or meet your experience more gently. "
5,Relaxation,Info-rlx-grp-02,"A familiar relaxation practice can feel different each day, including today. Approach it with curiosity, notice what feels supportive, and adapt as needed. "
6,Mindfulness,Info-mnd-grp-01,"Mindfulness can be like setting down a shaken snow globe: as the snow settles, the picture may become clearer. Notice whether this pause helps you reconnect with yourself and what matters to you. "
7,Mindfulness,Info-mnd-grp-02,"The present moment is never exactly the same, even when the practice is familiar. Choose one and meet this moment as it is - with today’s body, energy, and state of mind. "
8,Self-care,Info-sc-grp-01,"Self-care is also a process of discovery. Approach today’s choice with curiosity, without needing to know where the practice will take you. "
9,In the moment,Info-mmt-gme-01,"Pocket Practices can be used before or during social situations. Choose one and notice whether a brief pause helps you feel steadier, more present, or more connected."
10,In the moment,Info-mmt-gme-02,"Often, the most useful practices are the ones that fit easily into everyday life. Choose a Pocket Practice and notice what it brings. More steadiness? Focus? Calm? Something else"
11,In the moment,Info-mmt-gme-03,Some of the most useful practices are the ones small enough to carry into everyday life. Choose a Pocket Practice and notice where it might fit naturally into your day. 
12,Flexible thinking,Info-flx-grp-01,Our thoughts can have a big influence our experience. These practices can help create a little space and respond with flexibility and self compassion. Choose what feels like a good fit today.
13,Attention & emotional balance,Info-att-grp-01,What we give attention to can shape our experience. With these practices you can steady and guide your attention for greater emotional balance. Choose the one that feels useful today.
14,Cultivating calm,Info-cc-grp-01,"There are many ways to support the mind and body, cultivate calm, and release some tension. Choose what feels suitable and adapt the practice to how you are feeling today."
15,Meaningful action,Info-ma-grp-01,Meaningful action can begin with reconnecting to something that matters and finding one small way to move toward it that fits your life today.

1,Belly breathing,Info-brt-01,Belly breathing gives our attention a steady place to return while thoughts come and go. See if returning to the breath brings a little more clarity or quiet to the mind. 
2,Grounding,Info-grd-01,"Grounding offers a way to find a little more steadiness by gently returning attention to the body, the senses, and our surroundings. "
3,inner voice workout ,Info-ivw-gme-01,Our inner voice does not always tell the whole story. This practice can help us notice and step back from rigid or one-sided thoughts and make more room for a balanced perspective.
4,inner voice workout ,Info-ivw-gme-02,"This round helps us step back from all-or-nothing beliefs and take in a more flexible view of stress, relaxation and regulation."
5,inner voice workout ,Info-ivw-gme-03,Mindfulness can bring up many thoughts about how practice should feel. This round helps us step back from judgment and take in a more flexible perspective on whatever is here.
6,inner voice workout ,Info-ivw-gme-04,"Self-compassion can grow through practice. Each time we take in a kind and validating thought, we strengthen a more supportive inner voice."
7,inner voice workout ,Info-ivw-gme-05,"This round strengthens an inner voice that supports adapting, staying connected, and finding meaningful ways to participate."
8,inner voice workout ,Info-ivw-gme-06,"It is easy to get stuck in one way of seeing things. This practice helps us step back from one-sided thoughts, think more flexibly, and adopt a more balanced perspective."
9,cards game ,Info-crd-gme-01,"Self-regulation is not only about breathing or relaxation exercises. See if the cards bring to mind everyday things that help you pause, recharge, or feel a little steadier."
10,cards game ,Info-crd-gme-02,"This card game can also be a moment of mindfulness. Take your time with each card, approach it with curiosity, and notice what thoughts, feelings, or memories arise."
11,cards game ,Info-crd-gme-03,Connection can begin by sharing a small part of who we are. See if a card brings up something about yourself that you would enjoy remembering or sharing.
12,cards game ,Info-crd-gme-04,"Let this be a moment without any need to change anything. Approach the cards with a light touch and curiosity, and see what unfolds."
13,Mindful moment (pleasant exp),Info-mm-gme-01,"You might explore a pleasant moment of connection from the past week, or any other pleasant experience that comes to mind."
14,Mindful moment (pleasant exp),Info-mm-gme-02,"When discomfort is present, the mind naturally turns toward what feels difficult or threatening. This practice can help us make room for something pleasant. "
15,Mindful moment (gratitude),Info-mm-gme-03,"A moment of gratitude can be a simple act of self-care: bringing to mind something we appreciate, big or small, and allowing ourselves a moment to take it in. "
16,Mindful moment (this matters),Info-mm-gme-04,"What matters to us often shows up in small, everyday moments. This practice invites us to pause, notice one, and give it our attention."

PD Protocol Flow
March, 2026
Presentation Sub-title 2
Core principles 
1. Recommended Dosage of each module:

Module

2. First week of engagement should be focused on fundamentals (introductory videos and onboarding to games) and exposure of all types of contents and games, while minimizing choice. 

3. Medication reminders can be leveraged to engage in content related to diet and short form contents to enhance internalization.

4. If users stop items in the middle they can resume later on in the day. 

*Optional to think about - In case they engage with the app and choose not complete the entire agenda (we have to define how this would look like), we can think of adding short content fillers to increase the chance of completing the daily protocol.
 3
Physical Therapy
Learn:
1. A threshold of minimal viewing time will be defined. If user stops below the threshold, the same content will be displayed once(and not more than once) again.

Practice:
Multimodal Sessions – Each daily session follows a predefined structure and includes exercises from multiple modalities (strength, gait, flexibility, aerobics, and balance). There are no separate exercise flows dedicated to individual modalities.
Each sequence (daily exercise flow) will have 3 alternatives for the patient to choose, based on increasing difficulty level for the entire sequence
PT sessions are delivered every other day and do not occur on the same days as OT sessions.
Progression is based on block periodization mechanism, meaning that we would have 12-week monthly cycles that if progression is allowed if the user’s own progression measures permit, then the frequency, intensity and time of the sessions increase.
Progression measures:
Engagement with x% of sessions
Positive feedback by the user on a short checklist
The number of repetitions and/or time per exercise is predefined and cannot be modified by the user.
The movement score may inform decisions regarding when to unlock the next phase and recommend an appropriate level of complexity (reflected in different exercise alternatives).
Choice: User choice is expressed through the alternative options provided for each exercise. There is no option to select between entirely different exercises.
Other motor-related activities, such as walking or user-reported activities, do not influence the duration or structure of the PT sessions.

 4
Physical Therapy
Short form content will be given in a shorter version x weeks from the initial view to increase internalization 

Learn
Feedback from user will be presented when there’s an option to unlock the next phase / difficulty level. It will be comprised from a few items that the user will have to approve (thumb up). 
If approved – user moves to the next phase
If not approved – user stays in the same phase and the cycle is repeated again after a x days



Practice
האם לייצר בחירה בתחילת הרצף
האם האינטרו חייב להיות לאורך כל השימוש באפליקציה או שבשלבים מתקדמים אפשר לייצר חוויה כמה שיותר רציפה 5
Dance
Feedback from user will be collected to assess whether the user enjoys dancing.
Feedback will be collected after completing the first week of dance 
 In case user doesn’t enjoy dance and decide to opt out  – dance time will be replaced with extra time for PT
Choice:
user can choose to dance while being sitted if standing is difficult
User should have the option to practice the basic step only, without trying any alternatives
5. Stopping the dancing session in the middle doesn’t impact the next session.


Practice
Dance module should be introduced in week 2
Each week will be dedicated to a different dance and movement quality
3 sessions per week comprised of basic step and 1 or 2 alternatives on the basic step
לשקול אם הסשן הראשון בשבוע מכיל אך ורק את הצעד הבסיסי 6
Occupational Therapy
The module includes Learn (educational content, mainly strategies), Practice (fine motor exercises), Play (exergames).
Multimodal practice sessions – each practice session consists of exercises from multiple modals (Fine motor/dexterity, coordination and strength). There aren’t discrete exercise flows for each modality.
OT practice sessions are presented every other day, not on the days of PT.
Session duration is 5-10 min, with ~3 exercises per practice session.
Exercise progression model – TBD: In OT, there’s less emphasis on building strength or increasing the time of the exercise, the focus is on improving performace quality and on consistent practice. Therefore, we still need to determine whether exercises should progress over time, and if so, define progression parameters (e.g., difficulty level, duration, other parameters).
6. Personalizing based on difficulty levels: users either select difficulty level at the beginning of a practice session (like PT) OR users classify difficulty levels of exercises and sessions include a balanced mix of easy and challenging exercises.  7
Occupational Therapy
Content: mostly strategies videos (explanatory and practical, including modeled examples)
Feedback does not influence the protocol structure, it is there to help internalization
Short form content will be given in a shorter version x weeks from the initial view to increase internalization


Learn

Not final - Feedback from the user can be incorporated at the early stages of the protocol and be used for to clasiffy the difficulty level of the exerfcises by the users. 

Practice
Play
Choice:
Users are always given an option to choose from the set of fine motor games

~3 exercises per practice session in OT, ideally combining strength + coordination + dexterity
Suggested: OT every other day, not on the days of Physio 
Suggested to mix physio & Speech, OT & Dance, but also mixing and matching to not create too repetitive practice 
Implication of dexterity Score – TBD

Performance length usually increases the attention demand. 
1-2 min per exercise. 
Coins and teraplast might be longer. 

 8
Speech Therapy
The module includes Learn and Practice. 
All exercises are interactive and provide real-time feedback. For internal clarity, we group them into “warm-up” and “speech,” though therapy does not always label them this way.
The exercises are designed have progressively increasing demand, with defined levels and progression criteria based on performance analysis.
Still TBD:
Session structure: Will it alternate formats (warm-up + reading or warm-up + free speech) or including all the types of exercises in each session. Depends on the exercise's variety. 
Speech score & progression: 
Speech score implication on the protocol in general and on progression of the exercises. 
Speech score/performance analysis interaction with the user – when the user receives feedback, end of a level, end of practice, every specified period.
Will progression be also based on user feedback (similar to Physio; depends on how the exercise program will be structured)
“Warmup”:
If each warmup includes all components - amplitude, pitch glides (“bird”), and an automatic speech transition task (e.g., counting 1-10). 
If warm-up is fixed or personalized based on user baseline measures (e.g., maximum phonation time), which would require reassessment and adjusting the warmup during the protocol.

Learn
There will be an intro for each exercise, including for the “warmup” exercises, with the option to skip after the first times. 
Part of the intro will focus on proper posture and phone placement during practice, and guidance of proper performance.
Practice

How many exercises in aspeech session? 
Length of exercises, numberof reps, etc.

Users are instructed to play the maze 4 times a week, 15 min each time during weeks 1-4 and weeks 9-12
Users that don’t complete the 15 min block are encouraged to continue and play
Users who opt out of the game (define threshold of opting out) will be offered to play another intervention with a sensory subsitution feature - TBD 11
Psychology
Content types: self regulation techniques, attention training techniques, breathing, ACT, CBT, MBSR, MBCT
Feedback:
User who chooses not to interact with the activations
Remove intro content over time, offer the possibility to engage with it again if the users chooses to 
Reminders of the activations can be given either by the care coordinator or at the beginning of the next mindset session
For long term use- mindset is a set of activations only (without intro content) that is split into 4 different strips
Relaxation (self regulation, breathing)
Attention related (ATT and mindfulness)
Self, values (ACT, motivation)
Reflection – collect good moments and offer ability to go back and reflect on it- requires free text*
Choice: user can choose between the different strips of content



Mindset 12
Morning and Night Routine
Routines will be introduced to help habit formation. 
Morning routine will be aimed at reducing rigidity and will be comprised of motor, breathing techniques, setting intention for a good day
Night routine will be aimed at inducing good night sleep and will be comprised of ensuring sleep hygene, relaxation methods such as body scans and breathing techniques and reflection of the day that has passed
A couple of similar with slight differences routines will be introduced in order to keep them short (6-7 min each) and cover different type of activations
Routines will be part of the protocol only for 1 or 2 days and then moved to the library, with a widget on the home screen avialable at the relevant time of day,
Routines will be presented only in the relevant time of the day
Routines will be presented to the users incrementally, we will start with forming a morning routine and only when it moves to the library, we will present the night routine.
